content: Checkpoint navigation has an established offline and staleness vocabulary that this project should copy. indoor-mapping-wayfinding's degradation model: the engine degrades in order - latest validated graph, then last-known-good client cache, then a pre-baked immutable egress graph, then a 'Routing Unavailable' state - and 'an in-progress route is never torn down abruptly; the client finishes guidance on its cached graph and reconciles to the new topology'. The cache-coherence failure this prevents is the most damaging one: 'A user is routed into a loop because the client's cached graph still believes a removed edge is traversable', and a 'Routing Unavailable' fallback firing on a fully mapped floor because the metadata layer and the graph layer disagree - a split-brain cache state. The fix is a topology_hash per building/floor: clients store it, revalidate with a conditional request, and evict only the affected subgraph. Google's Navigation SDK FAQ models the same UX for a stale fix: show 'Searching for GPS...' after 10 seconds with no signal and hold the chevron at the last known point rather than pretending. The offline-first design-principles writeup gives the UI rules this project needs: an offline mode indicator with a data-freshness tooltip, a confidence badge (High/Medium/Low derived from last sync and cache hit rate), a local search fallback when the network cannot be reached, and 'staleness transparency - always show when data is stale and the estimated confidence of a route'. The strongest single rule comes from the offline-maps guidance: 'Static data that does not change between download and use - boarding passes, saved itineraries, offline maps of areas already cached - must never be gated behind a live connection check.' A floor plan and a graph are exactly that kind of static data, so a cached campus must remain fully usable with no network: search, map render and turn instructions must all work offline, and only the scan-to-server round trip needs connectivity.
